newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ssangyong sees loss falling in '97.
newsitem.headline: Ssangyong sees loss falling in '97.

text.p: Ssangyong Motor Co Ltd, an affiliate of South Korea's Ssangyong Group, expects its loss to narrow to 150 billion won in calendar 1997 from 228.5 billion won in 1996, a Ssangyong executive said.
Ssangyong Motor, a four-wheel-drive utility vehicle marker, set the 1997 sales target at two trillion won against sales of 1.37 trillion won in 1996, Cho Nam-do, vice president of the group, said.
"If the sales target is attained -- and I think it will -- the loss will shrink to 150 billion won this year," Cho told Reuters
He said sales of new "Korando" utility model and the planned introduction of "Chairman" luxury sedans would help improve the company's balance sheet.
Korando and Chairman models were developed with technical assistance from Mercedes-Benz, a subsidiary of Daimler-Benz AG
Cho said Ssangyong Motor was suffering from high debt-servicing costs as a result of heavy investment in the development of new models.
"We are seriously considering seeking foreign capital to help improve Ssangyong Motor's financial status," he said.
About half of the firm's 3.7 trillion won liabilities were short-term borrowings that should be repaid within a year and carry high interest.
Ssangyong Motor's total shareholders' equity dropped to 33.5 billion won at the end of 1996 from about 260 billion won at end-1995, due largely to huge losses, industry analysts said.
Cho said Ssanyong Motor was negotiating a strategic alliance with foreign firms, including three major U.S. carmakers. He declined to elaborate.

Other Ssangyong officials said General Motors Corp showed interest in using Ssangyong's sales network in South Korea, while Ssangyong hoped the U.S. company will provide capital and technology, particularly in developing compact passenger cars.

Shares of Ssangyong Motor went limit-up, gaining 450 won to 6,170 won in Thursday morning trading after rumours, denied by the companies, flared up again that the Samsung Group wanted to take over Ssangyong Motor, brokers said.
Cho said Ssangyong was not considering selling off the vehicle unit because of the current problems.
